source_text:
High-entropy alloys are among the most studied materials in modern solid-state physics and materials science. They can be defined as solid solutions of five or more elements with at least 5 atomic percent each. Their name derives from the high value of entropy of mixing, which is responsible for stabilizing simple structures (such as body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed) in these multicomponent materials. This is because increasing the amount of elements in a material usually leads to the precipitation of binary and ternary phases. In recent years, these materials have attracted considerable attention because of their remarkable mechanical properties; resistance to corrosion, including chemical corrosion; and stability over a wide temperature range. These features are due to the so-called HEA core effects described by Yeh et al..

Therefore, another consequence of these effects is the strong influence of internal chemical disorder and crystal lattice stresses on the superconducting properties of selected HEA alloys. Superconducting HEAs form a steadily growing family currently dominated by Nb-Ta matrices. There are also titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems, (which have some of the characteristics of HEAs). The formation of superconducting lanthanide-containing HEAs was first reported as early as 2015, but to date there is very little information on superconductivity in such systems. Recently, a paper about a superconducting partly ordered system containing heavy lanthanides was published, but there is no information about superconductivity in a system containing lanthanides which crystallize in a bcc structure.

queries.expert_context: Superconducting high-entropy alloys reported to date are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, with additional examples among titanium-rich heavy-transition-metal systems and partly ordered systems. Superconductivity in lanthanide-containing HEAs was first reported in 2015, and recent work examined a partly ordered system containing heavy lanthanides, but these precedents do not establish superconductivity in a lanthanide-containing system crystallizing in a bcc structure. Subject to the HEA definition of at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each and retention of the bcc state, what single intervention could yield superconductivity in such a starting material? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the unchanged bcc material, boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding literature, and a decisive experiment and result that would falsify it.
